chapter_theme: A single song at Tachur (தச்சூர்): the courtesan's flattering speech, which ranks the client above Murugan himself, and the poet's question whether he will go mad with desire for such women; the praise recalls Murugan teaching the poet 'the eighth letter'.

732.reading: The poet gives the courtesan's wheedling: she shows her breasts, aims her arrow-eyes, calls him 'cousin', says he made her long and then held back, that he stayed away that time and has no love for her, and that if one looks for his equal, even Kadamban falls short; with such talk she calls him her sugar, brings him home and lies with him on a grass mat, and the poet asks whether he will wander mad with desire for such women. The praise names the pearl who told 'the eighth letter' to the poor poet, the vel that cut down Sura's ranks, the adept who split him and made him peacock and cock, who fell at the hunter girl's feet and married her, and the lord of Tachur.
732.nuance: உனக்கு ஈடு பார்க்கில் கடம்பன் மட்டோ: the courtesan's flattery makes the client the equal of Murugan, an irony aimed at the poet who sings Murugan's praise. எட்டாம் எழுத்து ஏழையேற்குப் பகர்ந்த may refer to the poet's own initiation; which letter is meant (perhaps அ, which is also the Tamil numeral for eight) is not said. The opening of the praise (எச்சாய் மருட்பாடு ... பிச்சாசருக்கு) and the geography of the last lines are obscure to me.

links.note: In 732 the courtesan flatters the client that if one looks for his equal even Kadamban, Murugan, falls short (ஒப்பார் உனக்கீடு பார்க்கிற் கடம்பன் மட்டோ). Naladiyar 373 says such women would send away even the red-eyed Mal whom the gods worship if he had nothing in his hand to give (கொடுப்பதொன் றில்லாரை). The Naladiyar states the hidden condition of the flattery: the client is a god only while he pays.
